newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists snub, rap Socialist leader.
newsitem.headline: French Communists snub, rap Socialist leader.

text.p: France's Communist party criticised Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin on Friday for seeking to impose "hegemony" on the left and its official newspaper refused to publish his open letter to voters.
The snub was the latest sign of tension between the two left-wing opposition allies in the run-up to a snap May 25-June 1 parliamentary election called by President Jacques Chirac.
The Communist daily L'Humanite was one of the few newspapers which did not run Jospin's reply to Chirac's intervention in the campaign in support of the flagging centre-right coalition.
L'Humanite had however published the full text of Chirac's article attacking the left's record and programme on Wednesday.
"This sort of exchanges of letters turns the election into a sort of presidentialisation which is inappropriate," the outgoing Communist National Assembly floor leader Alain Bocquet said.
"It is desirable that the left which wins the parliamentary elections should be a balanced left. For the left to succeed, we need a more influential Communist party," he told RTL radio.

The Communists, who oppose a single European currency, were angered when Jospin pledged this week that if the left won, the Socialists would impose their favourable line on monetary union on their left-wing partners.
Communist leader Robert Hue hinted in a television interview on Thursday night that his party might make a referendum on the single currency its condition for supporting a Socialist-led government.

"We will have to negotiate taking account of the weight which each party will have received from voters, but without trying to align some behind others. I want to say formally that that is the condition for this left-wing majority to be possible," Hue said.

Political analysts said the Communists' highlighting of their differences with Jospin seemed mainly intended to deter their working-class electorate from voting Socialist on the first ballot for tactical reasons.
They noted that while Hue continued to press for a referendum, he had not specifically ruled out a single currency.
